Sustainable is a test the whole plan passes, not a label its products carry.

1
PETE: Good morning, we're Team Axis. I'm Pete. What makes a family's plan sustainable? Our case family asks for it as a share: twenty to twenty-five per cent of their savings in ESG products. But a label describes a product, not a plan. So we test the whole plan, twice. Outside in: does the plan last when climate hits? Inside out: what does the family's money change in the world? Take our client, the Wongs: a home, a packaging business, ten and a half million saved. In a sudden carbon shock, nearly half of what they'd lose lands on their home and business, where no fund share reaches. And every carbon cut we can measure is in the business, none in the funds. So our answer: sustainable is a test the whole plan passes, not a label its products carry. For the Wongs, that test changes six decisions, using HK$0.48M of the family's money and HK$1.91M of the business's, and cuts about 134 tonnes of carbon a year. Here's how we found them. PETE: How do we run those two tests? With PRISM. A green label gives one answer: yes or no. PRISM splits it into five questions. Profile: who decides, and within what limits. We set each person's limits, and a budget for their values, before we price anything. Risk is the first test, outside in: the whole family goes through one climate shock. Impact is the second, inside out: we count only real changes, never a cleaner-looking footprint. Select: every decision goes on one measure, green or not. Monitor: every decision comes with a trigger to look again. What comes out is one price tag for every decision: what it does for the children, in Hong Kong dollars, and what it does for the world, in tonnes. Then the limit decides. Here are the Wongs' six. PETE: Profile comes first. Adrian wants capital preservation; Carmen wants their money to reflect her values. Instead of arguing over every product, we settle it once. Their limit: the money must last their whole life in at least 95 futures out of 100. With plain choices, it lasts in 98. The gap, about 3, is the most their values may cost: their values budget, set before we price anything. Their choices, the ESG funds and the scholarship, use about 1. Adrian keeps his limit; Carmen spends inside it. [Notes: DRAFT, 13 Nov; Pete to make it his own. Wants: the case's words (Award2026Case, background). Limits ours (Final_Plan.md §4.2, ILLUSTRATIVE): 95 and 85 in 100 (Pete, 10 Nov). The budget (M9c, model_runs.md; fin_room_*): plain choices = plain funds (EDMW → IWDA, Allianz → AGGU, the cheapest MPF global equity fund), no giving, no vans; the room is 2.7 points before rounding. The choices = the ESG tilt's fees + the 20-year scholarship fund (≈0.9 points, HK$1.5M of the children's median inheritance). Under the 2030–31 scenario plain choices last in 92.2% against the crisis limit of 85, and the choices use 2.6 points, so the normal limit is the one that binds. If the scholarship is funded for 39 years (§5.3), the choices use ≈1.3 points. Tracking limits (Adrian ≤0.5% a year, Carmen ≤3%) are each person's own; the profile on the brief's seven dimensions is in research/area1_6_framework.md §3a, the rules for disagreement in §3c. The values budget is a mental account used on purpose, to lock the choice in advance (§4.2, biases). It builds on goals-based planning's aspirational bucket (Chhabra 2005; Das, Markowitz, Scheid and Statman 2010): cite it if asked.]

WIN: I'm Win. The S in PRISM is Select: every product runs through three gates. A binding, published rule. Measured and reported every year. And within the owner's risk budget. The fund from our earlier plan — BOC-Prudential — has zero assets at every filing. It fails at gate one. The fund that passes all three is EDMW, an iShares CTB ETF: it must stay thirty percent below its parent's carbon intensity and decline seven percent a year. That's a rule, not a label. Each parent's tracking-error budget sets how much ESG they can hold: Adrian's half-percent gives him thirty percent; Carmen's three percent gives her sixty. Weighted by their savings, the family share is twenty-seven point seven percent. It came out of the budgets — we didn't set it. The carbon numbers are sourced: WACI sixty-three, coverage ninety-nine point eight percent, ITR one band lower. But the portfolio avoids zero emissions. Secondary-market purchases finance nothing new. We say so. The price: about HK$0.57 million against plain twins over the plan's horizon — well within the values budget we set on slide four. And what we refused: a clean-energy fund, a green deposit, a sustainability-linked bond, and a green bond ETF. Each failed at least one gate. Every refusal is paired with what we do instead. WIN: The M in PRISM is Monitor. Our Climate Facts dashboard asks seven questions every year. Not a score — a set of answers, each with a trigger that says when the plan is wrong. Financial protection: ninety-seven percent odds to eighty-nine, checked against material life changes. Values price: the HK$0.57 million gap we just showed, reconciled whenever fees or mandates change. Operations: Carmen's baseline in 2027 — we can't claim a reduction until we've measured the starting point. Alignment: the portfolio's WACI and coverage, checked whenever the fund's method changes. Outcome: no causal result yet, and we say so. When evidence is missing, we qualify the claim — we don't drop it. And every missing price becomes one of three decisions: buy the answer now, accept a range, or set a trigger. The fund call is a buy: we check EDMW quarterly. ESG under stress is a range: the CTB index should lose less in a carbon-price shock, but nobody's measured it, so we give it no credit. Recycled PET is a trigger: at parity we switch; at a ten percent premium we pay; above that, we refuse. Pete will show you what happens when the plan meets reality.
